top_cited_works.title: Commonly Used Disinfectants Fail To Eradicate Salmonella enterica Biofilms from Food Contact Surface Materials
top_cited_works.abstract: Salmonellosis is the second most common cause of food-borne illness worldwide. Contamination of surfaces in food processing environments may result in biofilm formation with a risk of food contamination. Effective decontamination of biofilm-contaminated surfaces is challenging. Using the CDC biofilm reactor, the activities of sodium hypochlorite, sodium hydroxide, and benzalkonium chloride were examined against an early (48-h) and relatively mature (168-h) Salmonella biofilm. All 3 agents result in reduction in viable counts of Salmonella; however, only sodium hydroxide resulted in eradication of the early biofilm. None of the agents achieved eradication of mature biofilm, even at the 90-min contact time. Studies of activity of chemical disinfection against biofilm should include assessment of activity against mature biofilm. The difficulty of eradication of established Salmonella biofilm serves to emphasize the priority of preventing access of Salmonella to postcook areas of food production facilities.

top_cited_works.title: Post Injections for Soot Reduction in Diesel Engines: A Review of Current Understanding
top_cited_works.abstract: This work is a technical review of past research and a synthesis of current understanding of post injections for soot reduction in diesel engines. A post injection, which is a short injection after a longer main injection, is an in-cylinder tool to reduce engine-out soot to meet pollutant emissions standards while maintaining efficiency, and potentially to reduce or eliminate exhaust aftertreatment. A sprawling literature on post injections documents the effects of post injections on engine-out soot with variations in many engine operational parameters. Explanations of how post injections lead to engine-out soot reduction vary and are sometimes inconsistent or contradictory, in part because supporting fundamental experimental or modeling data are often not available. In this paper, we review the available data describing the efficacy of post-injections and highlight several candidate in-cylinder mechanisms that may control their efficacy. We first discuss three in-cylinder mechanisms that have been frequently proposed to explain how post injections reduce engine-out soot. recent_works.title: Prediction and Measurement of the Dynamics of Multi-Element Wake Flows
recent_works.abstract: Wake flows can display a global instability that results in large-scale, anti-symmetric vortex shedding. Several prior studies have shown that the dynamics of this wake shedding can vary significantly in multi-element flows, where multiple wakes are placed side by side. The frequency, symmetry, and intermittency of wake shedding are highly dependent on the spacing between wakes and the number of wakes. The goal of this study is to map the dynamics of multi-element wake systems as a function of the number of wakes, wake spacing, and Reynolds number using two methods. First, we use a simplified linear stability analysis of piecewise flow profiles to predict the frequency, growth rate, and symmetry of the oscillations over a large range of these parameters. A similar parameter study is also done experimentally in a new facility. Stereo high-speed particle image velocimetry is used to measure the flow, and modal analyses, like spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and wavelet analysis, are used to capture the flow dynamics. recent_works.title: A Framework for Understanding the Impact of Fuel Composition on Flame Heat Transfer to Materials
recent_works.abstract: Gas turbine hot section materials experience extreme environments with high heat loads. Several recent studies in representative combustor configurations have shown that convective and radiative heat transfer contributions can vary significantly depending on flow features and fuel composition. In this work, we use a fundamental burner configuration to better understand the impact of fuel composition and material properties on heat transfer to hot section materials. A new framework allows the separation of convective and radiative contributions through heat-flux measurements, chemical kinetic modeling, and one-dimensional modeling of convective and radiative heat transfer. Material samples were mounted to a heat-flux block above a standard flat-flame McKenna burner, and heat flux was measured using a one-dimensional thermal network derived from a thermocouple array embedded in the insulated block. A large test matrix that includes variations in adiabatic flame temperature, product mole fraction of carbon dioxide, and product mole fraction of water was tested with blends of methane and hydrogen in various oxidizers. recent_works.title: Using Reactor Networks for Predicting the Impact of Turbine Expansion on Gas Turbine Emissions
recent_works.abstract: The goal of this study is to develop a chemical reactor network model to understand the impact of turbine expansion on engine-out emissions. Historically, experimental studies and network models measure combustor-out emissions, but the rapid expansion in the turbine, which results in dramatic reductions in temperature and pressure, could have an impact on kinetics with slow timescales, including pollutant formation and recombination reactions. The combustor model consists of a series of perfectly stirred reactors representing the primary, recirculation, and dilution zones of a gas turbine combustor. The test case used in this study is based on prior studies that considered the use of exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) with carbon capture and hydrogen enrichment in the fuel as two methods to reduce the carbon emissions from industrial and power generation gas turbines. Different blends of diluents are used to simulate EGR with oxygen from 21% to 15% by volume and carbon dioxide addition up to 15% by volume. recent_works.title: Critical Regions Driving Unsteady Wake Dynamics in Flow Past Multi-Cylinder Arrays
recent_works.abstract: Large-eddy simulation (LES) is used to determine the time-resolved flow evolution past two cylinders placed side by side. The simulations are conducted at a nominal Reynolds number of Re = 10,000. Complex network analysis is applied to the resulting datasets to identify the location and spatial extent of the flow regions that govern the unsteady wake dynamics. A nominal single-cylinder configuration with well-established reference data is employed to benchmark the LES. For the closely spaced two-cylinder case, an asymmetric time-averaged flow structure with a biased inter-cylinder gap flow is observed. This configuration exhibits a broad and a narrow wake, with the former driving the vortex shedding in the near wake. The widely spaced case presents a symmetric time-averaged flow structure, with vortex shedding from both wakes that interact further downstream.
